Let us find out how she is doing in national defence before we give her the responsibility of the country. I would like to know that and I know other Canadians would like to know that. I bet there are some members on that side of the House who would like to know that. I make no apologies for that, although in the first instance my concern and the concern of my party is based on the legitimate difficulties that we observed from looking at this case in detail, the case of peacekeeping and the incidents in Somali that have shown less than good, strong leadership, the kind that we need in this country.
On the helicopter issue I want to say that there are as many red flags on the EH-101 as there are in peacekeeping. I just want to make one comment in response to something that was said over there. My good friend, the member for Halifax West talked about the number of jobs. I have a report from an expert organization that says for every billion dollars spent on military procurement, 28,000 jobs are generated. If you spent it on public transportation you would get 32,000 jobs. If you spent it on infrastructure you would get 57,000. If you spent it on education you would get 71,000. Whatever arguments are put forward, do not put that one forward because it does not make sense.
In conclusion, my point is the issues are raised about the credibility of the minister for good reasons. I say they are not partisan reasons. They are certainly not from anything I have said this morning. We need a public debate on peacekeeping and how we do business because of the changing factors involved. We need a public debate on how we acquire major equipment for the Department of National Defence again because of these changing issues.

Madam Speaker, I have a comment and a question for the member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception. Let me say to him first that we all come to this House of Commons from
different backgrounds. I appreciate that his background is in the defence field and that he has had a very important career in Canada's military. But when he comes to the House of Commons and says "nothing I say today, none of my remarks, reflect adversely on the credibility of the Canadian Armed Forces or the officers, men and women of the Canadian Armed Forces", that is a caveat that does not wash.
The member must know, as we all know, that the Minister of National Defence acts upon the advice of the military officers. The chief of the Canadian forces, the assemblage of high ranking officers are continually advising the minister and nobody has suggested that the Minister of National Defence in any of these areas has acted on advice other than the advice of the military.
While it is generous of the member to announce to the House of Commons that nothing reflects adversely on the military in his remarks, he knows and the military knows that that kind of criticism does reflect adversely on the Canadian forces when it is suggested that the policies being followed have dire results. He knows and we all know that those policies are based upon the advice of the military, including the chief officers of the military.
Because he only had 30 seconds to deal with the EH-101 helicopter contract, he confined himself to a remark about the industrial spin-offs in employment. I want to remind him that a billion dollars in unemployment insurance would keep a lot of people happy. What we are trying to do as a government is balance government expenditures to produce the services required for the Canadian people as well as create employment. It is not to create employment that the EH-101 helicopter contract is being promoted and implemented. It is to serve the Canadian forces and the national defence interests of Canada.
If the member wants to make a comment about the helicopter contract and other matters he should simply state what his view is on that particular contract on the equipment of the Canadian forces, whether it is necessary. Does he agree, for example, with his colleague from Winnipeg South Centre who says we must change the policy, that we do not need helicopters, we may not even need patrol frigates because we are not going to be attacked.
April 29, 1993

Supply
That is what I want to ask the member, not whether he quarrels with the industrial spin-off, not whether he quarrels with the quality of the contract, the nature of the equipment, but whether he believes we do not need a Canadian navy any more and we do not need patrol frigates and we do not need helicopters. What is his position on that issue?
I would like also to deal with the matter of our policy in Somalia. I simply want to say this, and perhaps the member might want to comment on it.
On the highways and streets and roads of Somalia we cannot judge our Canadian Armed Forces' members by Canadian standards that prevail in the cities and towns of Canada. We cannot simply expect them to behave exactly as they would on Wellington Street or the streets of St. John's, Newfoundland or Halifax, Nova Scotia. Our laws do not have extraterritorial application. We simply must judge them and exercise jurisdiction over them in the manner endorsed by law, and that law is the National Defence Act and that law has been followed in this case.
I also want to know whether the member quarrels with that. Would he have the Ontario Highway Traffic Act apply on the streets of Somalia to Canadian Armed Forces' drivers? Is that his intention? I want him to understand and I want everybody to understand that we cannot judge our forces by prevalent urban city standards in Canada.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member who is normally very cogent seems to have fallen out of the track this morning. He has covered a wide range of issues, from the responsibility of national defence to the highways act in Ontario, to helicopters and the responsibilities of the minister.
Before I answer his questions, I want to tell him that I presume he has misunderstood what was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. He did not say that we did not need patrol frigates; he did not say we did not need a navy; and if the hon. member had had a difficulty with what the member for Winnipeg South Centre had said, I wish he had put those questions to him when he was in the House and not to me after the hon. member had to leave to keep an important appointment in Winnipeg.
The other thing I want to say to the hon. member-
He left right after his speech.

It is a distortion anyway, that is my point.
I want to address one aspect of what the hon. member for Halifax West said. It is absolutely incredible that he suggested that the Minister of National Defence does what the minister is told by the department. That is absolutely incredible. The minister, under the National Defence Act, is charged with management and direction. That is her responsibility. How can one give direction if one always follows what one is told?
I happen to be aware of one Minister of National Defence who was briefed on the acquisition programs of the Canadian Armed Forces. He was told by the senior members that Canada could not afford nuclear submarines. That particular minister directed the Canadian forces to conduct a study to determine whether nuclear submarines were possible. That is the kind of direction I would expect the minister to give. That is the kind of direction we would expect any minister to give, including this minister.
If the hon. member closely looked at the point he raised, if he is suggesting that the Minister of National Defence parrots everything that is said to her by the department then we may have some evidence to support the suggestion in the motion that she suffers a lack of leadership and direction.
I am going to be kind to the member and suggest that any minister worth his or her salt in any department would not just follow the information given to that minister by the department. Presumably it is a two-way conversation, a two-way exchange of information.
I still find it incredible that the minister on March 17 would have been briefed by national defence officials about the serious incident and not have been briefed on the public relations aspect, on whether or not there should be a media release in Canada. That I do not understand. I do not credit the department with that. Whatever advice was given, whether it was positive or negative, the minister should have said that this is a serious incident, and I believe I am on firm ground here. If she had known about the incident on March 4, which was an equally serious incident, she should have at least said: We have not heard too much about the March 4

April 29, 1993
Supply
incident but we had better now do something about this incident because it is similar.
Whatever happened, whether the minister directed that media release be given, whether she directed that the Canadian public be informed, it did not take place. She did not inform the Canadian public until the news story broke. Everybody was kept in the dark and the information leaked out.
That does not show good leadership, in the evidence or the results, no matter what went on. I suppose we will never know the story about what happened exactly.
Did the minister do what was recommended by national defence or did the minister give direction that (a) it not take place, that Canadians not be informed, or (b) that whatever direction was taken she agreed with national defence?
I have no problems with a board of inquiry being conducted by any officer in the Canadian forces. With a major-general conducting a board of inquiry no Canadian would have any difficulty in believing, and rightfully so, that the information would be anything but objective. However that inquiry, by the veiy nature of what sparked it in this House, goes outside the military. How can we expect a major-general to inquire into the conduct of a minister? It does not happen.
We are suggesting that there be a public inquiry where these facts will be brought out to the public, not at the end of July but as they occur. We need to know now. This is not going to die. The media will continue to probe and the Canadian public will continue to ask questions.
My response to the hon. member is that I believe he has some of his information wrong. He has certainly distorted the information that was given by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre in his speech. If what he believes about the minister is true then he is agreeing with the motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when I was informed last night about this debate today I found myself in a veiy difficult position.
It is no secret in this House and in other places that these days I am quite closely associated with the Minister
of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs in her quest to become Prime Minister of this country.
My initial reaction to this particular motion and the way it was put forward was anger. I wrote eight or nine speeches in my mind over a period of three or four minutes and realized that was probably not the best approach to take.
In considering whether I wanted to participate in this debate I worried very much about bringing the campaign and process that so many very capable people in my party have offered to participate in, and for which they have offered themselves to this party and this country, into this House. That would not be a good idea either.
I did not want to take advantage of this opportunity to promote my particular choice over the others. I feel very strongly about the choice I have made. However I also feel very strongly that every one of those candidates from this institution would make a tremendous leader of my party and my country.
I thought about it more in the context of what is happening here politically and what it means for us as a government to support the Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs in the job that she does. I debated with some of my friends and my colleagues in the minister's office and in the House leader's office about whether I would participate.
By this morning I had calmed myself down. As I started to think about this debate and about the process that has been going on here in terms of the way this House has been forced to deal with this issue, it became perfectly obvious to me that this House has not been asked to deal with the issue in terms of national defence and the management of a government department. It is about the desire of some people to make political points, and not just on the back of the Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs or the House leader but potentially if there is an environmental issue, on the back of the Minister of the Environment, et cetera.
This is on the backs of the people caught in the middle of this, the soldiers, the men and women, the regular forces and reservists who are serving not only in Somalia but in Bosnia and 17, 18, 19, or 20 other theatres around
April 29, 1993

the world. To some extent they accept some of these risks. It is also on the backs of the families.
There are about 1,100 men and women from this country in Somalia. I have not been to Somalia. I have spent a fair bit of time in Ethiopia, Eritrea, Sudan and 16 or 17 countries to the west of that. I can imagine what Somalia is like. I have not been in a war situation. I have been in some civil war situations in which there have been firings and shootings. I have been in military operations in Central America.
To a family that is sitting in Petawawa or St. John's, Newfoundland whose mother, sister, father, brother, son or daughter has gone off in a plane to a land people have no concept of, to a situation that people can only imagine, where there have been incidents-and sure there have been incidents. There are 1,100 people there, 845 of them from the airborne division. It is a very tense situation in a very hostile land with a very hostile environment and a very hostile political climate.
The men and women who are left here to worry about their loved ones are all of a sudden confronted with the perception out of this place that every single one of them over there has been involved in some sort of violent or untoward incident. In the process of trying to attack this government and the Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs we have completely forgotten those people.
Day after day outside this place, when the minister is not here, when the opposition is attacking the military generally from Colonel By Drive to the last buck private in Somalia there is no recognition that those people left behind make as much of a sacrifice and contribution in their own way. That is the shame of it. It is not the attacks on the Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs, the House leader, the Prime Minister or the Deputy Prime Minister. After the last eight years they are used to it in this place. However the abuse that is going on here is being heaped on top of those who are scared to death.
Preserver was over there. We remember the gulf war and Protecteur and Preserver. Thirty per cent of those people were Newfoundlanders. A lot of them had addresses that said they were from Dartmouth but many
Supply
of those men and women serving on ships were Newfoundlanders. I was quite close to one family. I know what that mother went through every single day watching the television with her hands over her eyes but her fingers open because she did not want to miss anything. She knew in her mind that her son was okay and was going to be okay. The risks were there but they were minimal, but in her heart she did know what was going to happen next.
We get this resolution today. We get this opposition day motion clearly attacking the Minister of National Defence on her performance and what has gone on here and what has gone on there. I hear my friend, a former senior officer in the military, talking to me about credibility, about the credibility of the minister and the government. I want to address some of those points because they are important.
The minister, the House leader, the Prime Minister, the chief of defence staff, and a variety of spokespersons for the Department of National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces have repeatedly put forward the incidents as they happened and the responses that went with them. Nobody has denied there have been problems.
I go back to Somalia and what we are dealing with there in a big international organization. Nobody has denied there have been questions about communications. What we have to put in context is what went on and what did not go on, and what gets said in this House about nobody knowing. I am not going back through it. It has been gone through already.
We are talking about credibility. We get a statement in this House that after the incident on March 4 nobody said or did anything. On the morning of March 5 it was on bloody Newsworld.
With all due respect, even for somebody like me who still remembers Don Jamieson doing the news with a Chevrolet car in the studio, I recognize that Newsworld is the news. Do not talk to me about credibility.
My colleague from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception was a commanding officer on more than one ship. He had very serious responsibilities in terms of maritime command and a number of different things.

April 29, 1993
Supply
Imagine that if every time there was an incident-I am not making this one seem smaller than it may be-the minister was on the phone to him saying: "Admiral, get the press release out. Admiral, I am going to be talking in the House of Commons this afternoon about what happened on the bridge of your ship last week or on the lower deck of your ship last week".
The Solicitor General of Canada does not come into this House every time there is an investigation conducted by the RCMP. The Minister of National Defence has never and should never come into this House to talk about every time there is an investigation, particularly of this nature, going on where the military is functioning.
It is clearly the responsibility of the Department of National Defence to ensure that people are kept informed. The process has been followed. The minister addressed it in her statement earlier this week in terms of the action that the department undertook to keep people informed.
In most of those cases people were kept informed. Incidents were reported. The minister quite clearly acknowledged that she knew there had been an incident. She did not know that there had been a homicide. How did she find out? The department instigated an investigation as the department should do.
We talked about management and direction. The minister has quite clearly said that there have been some problems with communications. She has ordered that they be fixed and that whatever information can be made public be made public.
Why would I say something like: "Whatever can be made public should be made public"? If there is a criminal investigation under way then first one wants to be able to finish it. Second, one does not want to prejudice the investigation and those who unfortunately may be subject to that investigation.
Perhaps we have a problem in that the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Veterans Affairs used to be the Minister of Justice. She knows how the justice system works and must work. She understands her responsibilities within that.
There was an inquiry. It was a military inquiry with public participation. How did we get public participation in that sort of inquiry? The minister ordered that the
regulations be amended. This is the sort of management and direction that my friend talks about.
The results of that inquiry will be made public as the chief of defence staff explained yesterday. The people will know what has gone on through that process. People will know that this sort of thing happened for a particular set of reasons. They will also know that the investigation that as I say unfortunately must go on will not be prejudiced by the inquiry.
I am very worried as I said in the beginning that my friends opposite have lost totally the focus. I heard some of the comments this morning of the member for Winnipeg South Centre. I have heard that sort of thing before: the desperation, the personal attacks and the bitterness. We have come to expect a little bit of it from time to time.
We have had to make some decisions in the process that the Minister of National Defence has pursued. She found herself spending more time on the telephone dealing with national defence matters, as she should and she must, that made it practical at the end of last week to continue conducting her political business that is part of her responsibility as a minister.
She returned to Ottawa and met on Friday and Sunday I think with officials of her department. She appeared in this House and with the Secretary of State for External Affairs took questions in this House. In areas related to the United Nations the Secretary of State for External Affairs rightly responded to these. In the areas that pertained to defence the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Veterans Affairs responded to these.
She was again in this House on Tuesday. This opposition that wanted her so badly in this House to bring her to account asked one insipid, stupid question about her schedule. She sat there prepared to respond. She did interviews and responded to the media but there was not one question in the House.
When she is again out of town we come beating on the door. These great, valiant troopers are defenders of the people on whose backs they have tromped to make trite political points. When they really want to do some business and they have the minister here they are scared to death. They will not stand up in front of her and say:
April 29, 1993

"Minister, account for yourself" because she will bury them like she buried them on Tuesday afternoon.
The minister and this government, with the help of the House leader and the Prime Minister and all of her colleagues, have respected the military in this country and the role that we ask them to play, which in many cases is a bloody awful role and one that a lot of us would not do ourselves. One leaves one's family. We have some experience with that when we come to the battlefields of Ottawa. They are in deserts in Somalia and the heat of the Middle East, Pakistan and India and around the world. We impugn every one of them and we impugn their senior officers. Those who have been at fault in this will be found out, as well they should be, and dealt with fairly, equitably and justly within the criminal justice system of this country and the military.
However, let us not forget those who they have left behind and let us not leave them behind in our attempt to make some points as we go along.
I am tempted not to talk about the helicopters but I have not talked about the helicopters except on the late show. I have to say that I had some concerns about the helicopters like many others and like my friends across the way. I will say that I will continue to watch as it plays itself out because there have been some commitments made. I am very intrigued to know that we should get 15 per cent of the economic benefit of the helicopters in Atlantic Canada.
Frankly, I am most concerned about the capacity of Canada to protect those who make their living and make their income from the sea. A number of us, and none more than my friend from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception, have been confronted with the tragedies that happen at sea where people need to be protected and people need their lives saved. It is the nature of what we do.
The capacity of the current equipment simply is not there. What we are offering today is not good enough, particularly when there is better equipment available that is made in this country and will be made and sold from this country.
This is perceived to be some great Tory plot. I think we have to recognize that what we are doing is replacing our rapidly aging fleet over a period of more than 13 years within the context of the shrinking national defence
Supply
budget. These are decisions that have been made by the Department of National Defence.
This is something that is not simply supported by us. I have a letter here from the mayor of the town of Gander, His Worship Doug Sheppard. I am not sure of his political persuasion and I certainly would not want to assign any unjustly. He quite clearly supports the helicopters and there are others.
I simply want to say in closing as it relates to the helicopters that it is not as cut and dried as everybody thinks. It is not $4.5 billion next year and that is it and we have helicopters. As we analyse both these issues we have to be open and fair and remember from where we have come. My biggest concern is for those who serve in the military and particularly their families and what we put them through. They are doing jobs that I, like many of my colleagues, probably would not do. I am very sad to see this day come where we have taken this type of advantage.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have listened with great interest to my colleague opposite. I must say that in the time that I have spent in this Chamber, which has been going on in excess of 10 years in this great institution, I have never heard such gobbledegook and such distortion of the facts and the truth.
I have respect for the hon. member and what he has said. It does not necessarily mean that I agree with what the hon. member has said. The first point that the hon. member must recognize is that it was said clearly and unequivocally earlier this day that no one on this side of the House would dispute the fact that the Minister of National Defence has the right, and maybe the obligation, to seek the highest office in this land. No one has argued with that.
Equally so, the hon. member stands in his place and casts aspersions on those of us who sit in opposition to this administration for raising questions and for asking for debate only to be turned down at each and every opportunity. The purpose of today's debate is simply to discuss the issues and obviously the major issue of the day is the incompetence persistently and consistently of the minister responsible. This could have been avoided if clearer heads had prevailed and particularly if ministers opposite had taken the subject matter seriously and come into this House under ministerial statements-not after the fact but well before.

April 29, 1993
This hon. member from Bonavista-Trinity has been calling repeatedly and consistently for debate on the subject matter with regards to the training of our peacekeepers. That member over there has the unmitigated gall to question and to impugn the motives of that hon. member and this opposition party. I say to that hon. member that there is not a bone in his body that will not testify to the fact that the only reason he is here today to speak to this motion is because he happens to be the co-campaign manager for the Minister of National Defence and he is trying to protect that minister. That is the only reason the hon. member is here.
Madam Speaker, I am coming to my question. The hon. member said that on Tuesday we only had one question. It was the day after the budget, as the hon. member knows. The hon. Minister of National Defence had our resolution last night when she was here for the vote. I asked my colleagues to return to Ottawa to participate in this debate. Why?
I ask the hon member, why is it that no minister of the Crown is here, particularly the Minister of National Defence, nor the Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Associate Minister of National Defence to stand for the Armed Forces and give us more details with regard to the situation? I will tell you why, Madam Speaker.

AFTER RECESS

Mr. Speaker, it was with great regret that I and the people involved in the forestry
industry in Prince Edward Island heard the Minister of Finance announce that our regional development agreement for forestry would not be renewed.
The agreement, which expired on March 31, 1993 was worth over $24 million to the forestry industry in P.E.I. and was responsible for the creation of over 500 jobs in planting seedlings, harvesting and hauling the logs. In addition it fostered the growth of forests, management techniques and silviculture in general.
The industry had been negotiating in good faith to get a renewed agreement and was left with the impression that the only issue to be resolved was the length of the agreement. To suddenly find it was cancelled was, to put it mildly, a shock. Other provinces have had their agreements renewed. P.E.I. will be the only province negatively impacted by the budget decision.
I remind the minister of a statement made by him at the Standing Committee on Forestry and Fisheries in November 1990. He said:
I remain committed to the continuation of the development
agreements as an essential instrument of the sustainable development
of our forest resource.
After having met with the minister in committee and privately and discussing the situation with ACOA, I have every confidence that the minister's sense of justice and fair play will prevail and he will not allow P.E.I.'s forestry industry to be sandbagged in this fashion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to inform hon. members that the week of April 26 to May 1 has been declared Allergy Awareness Week and May has been declared Allergy Awareness Month.
Every year the Allergy Foundation of Canada chooses a week to highlight the problem of allergies and to show what can be done to relieve them. This volunteer-led organization provides information and support for people suffering from this problem.
The cost of allergy-related illnesses, in terms of health care and lost productivity, is huge and growing all the time. In addition, the social cost is incalculable.
April 29, 1993

I wish the Allergy/Asthma Information Association every success for Allergy Awareness Month.

Mr. Speaker, the departure of the Minister of National Health and Welfare opens a vacuum of leadership on medicare in the Tory ranks. Despite his bungling of some key health issues the departing minister was at least on record as supporting universal medicare and he spoke out against user fees.
Where do the Tory leadership candidates stand today? In the shade. They have not come forward to back the Canada Health Act and the five principles of medicare, the most loved of all social programs.
I fear they intend to end universality and will continue to cut medicare funding to the provinces, even though from Manitoba and beyond the medicare system is in crisis.
I fear they will impose user fees as they voted to do so at the last Tory convention. I fear they will allow privatization of medicare.
Why do the Tory candidates, the defence minister, the environment minister and others, not tell us the real plans for the Canada Health Act, the underpinning of our universal medicare?
Keep it or kill it, which will it be?

Mr. Speaker, I met recently with a group of aviation workers from the riding I represent who have expressed concern for the future of Canada's airline industry.
Recognizing that the airline industry in Canada is at a crossroads with the proposed alliance between Canadian Airlines and American Airlines, the aviation workers expressed concern that Canada will be viewed by U.S. mega-carriers as a secondary market. As a result, service will suffer and jobs will be lost.
I believe that the best interests of Canadians are served if our country has a fully Canadian airline, not an
airline that is an offshoot of a foreign-owned mega-carrier.
The Canadian market can support one viable internationally competitive carrier. As a result, jobs in management and reservations, aircraft maintenance and support services could be preserved.
Gemini Corporation has the technology to provide reservation services and we have skilled workers in every area of the airline industry.
I believe that Canadians should be served by one Canadian airline owned and operated by Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, Liberals say one thing when they are in opposition and did another when they were in government. The Liberals have joined the New Democratic caucus in calling for open public hearings on the tragic deaths in Somalia.
The Liberals have acted outraged that the government should be so undemocratic as to reject a full public inquiry into this matter. The Liberals want Canadians to believe that they would be more open about dealing with scandals than this shameful crop of Conservatives.
However the Liberals did not feel so strongly about openness when they were in government. Ten years ago in this House of Commons I asked the Liberal government to hold public hearings into the Atomic Energy Control Board's decision to increase the allowable level of radiation exposure to pregnant women by five times the current rate. The Liberal energy minister repeatedly refused to allow public hearings into this matter. Who was that minister? None other than the current Liberal leader.

Mr. Speaker, in a move that showed no heart or understanding for the people of the tri-towns last Friday, the provincial NDP government saw fit to slash at the already crippled economy of Timiskaming.
One of the casualties of the NDP that makes no sense is the closing of the New Liskeard Agricultural College.

April 29, 1993
This 26-year old institution has 120 students and over 50 employees at the facility. In the last three to four years about $12 million worth of new buildings has been added. It is no secret that New Liskeard's college greatly contributes to the province's agricultural advancement.
The research centre and laboratory, which services from Parry Sound through to the Manitoba border, focuses both on crop and livestock technology. It is also a research facility for sheep and beef in Ontario. Programs at the college, through an outreach program, are offered across the north and range from engineering and business management to horticulture and crop science.
This facility has a tremendous impact on our community, injecting $1.3 million into the economy. I say to Bob Rae, on behalf of the residents of Timiskaming, that this facility should be saved. Its continued service is essential for the region and for Ontario farmers.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian seniors are fighting back. In a column in The Ottawa Citizen Madeleine Honeyman says: "Political abuse of the elderly is making Granny grumpy". She goes on to say:
It is far from proven to my satisfaction that the over 70s use more of the health-care dollar than the very young-It is also questionable whether the old take more from the social system than they pay to support our overloaded education system, welfare for young people who haven't been able to find jobs and mortgage payments for their middle-aged children and grandchildren who are out of work.
Perhaps it is time all Canadians remember who started our medicare system, who built and paid for our hospitals, who paid to educate our doctors, our nurses and our researchers and who paid to put in place our pension system. Who else but seniors are charged 100 per cent on their income in taxes?
Madeleine Honeyman concludes by saying, and she means this: "Beware, Granny is getting leaner and meaner".

Mr. Speaker, on February 19, 1993, I had the opportunity to visit the new premises of the Federal Office of Regional Development (Quebec) and Forestry Canada in Val d'Or. At a time like this when all departments must reduce their spending, I wish to congratulate the management of these two departments on this initiative of combining and sharing services.
This new government service centre will save large amounts in operating expenses, will improve customer service and promote synergy between these two organizations.
In conclusion, I want to point out that the presence of these two departments is essential for promoting the economic development of western Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, the finance minister dealt more blows to western Canada in his most recent budget. Unfortunately westerners have come to expect this from this particular government but it is particularly painful when it comes from a fellow westerner.
Fully $27 million was cut from the Western Economic Diversification Fund, something that is vital to the development of products, technology and industry in our region. The Crow benefit was cut last December and now further cuts are promised. Another $250 million is scheduled to be cut from the CBC by 1998. It is dear the present government's intent is to kill the CBC slowly. That would spell disaster for many westerners who watch the CBC in order to have valuable information.
VIA Rail also faces a $250 million cut by 1998. This is also of concern to westerners. Will we end up having VIA trains only between Windsor and Quebec City? Is that the intent of this government, this unloved govern-
April 29, 1993

ment? It is ironic that railway passenger service was what united this country initially and now those opposite are trying to destroy that along with so many other institutions in Canada.

subtopic: MINISTER OF FINANCE OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
MINISTER OF FINANCE OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in typical NDP fashion the finance minister of British Columbia has condemned the federal budget. Mr. Clark is the only finance minister in Canada who has not seen the light and moved to reduce spending and cut the cost of government.
While everyone else in the country is attempting to reduce costs and hold the line on taxes, Mr. Clark and the NDP Government of B.C. have increased their budget by 5.6 per cent. He has increased taxes, increased the size of government and the complexity of government. He has hired hundreds of new civil servants.
At the same time the minister is whining that he should be getting more money from the federal government. My constituents tell me that we should not give him any increase at all until he recognizes the economic facts of life and mends both his own and his government's profligate ways.

Mr. Speaker, today's Globe and Mail quotes statements of East York Councillor John Papadakis in a context that implies that any refugee claimant may be bogus, any immigrant may be illegal and persons who commit crime on our streets may be refugees or immigrants from certain countries whose people appear in Canada as visible minorities.
This is unjust, since he does not show evidence that refugees or immigrants have a higher crime rate than those who are Canadian bom. He is also quoted as objecting to refugee claimants receiving welfare.
In fact, municipal authorities and both opposition parties urged the government in recent amendments to the Immigration Act to allow refugee claimants to work. However, the government insisted on forcing them onto welfare to survive. Maybe the government will reconsider that unfortunate decision.

Mr. Speaker, in my view one of the most important measures in the budget announced by the Minister of Finance on Monday is the strong commitment to collaborative financial planning with the provinces of Canada.
It is my hope that the consultations which will take place at the meeting of finance ministers in May will not only deal in broad terms of debt and deficits, as essentially they must. It is also imperative that their deliberations touch on matters of fundamental political policy and principle.
For example, there is insistent pressure to change and diminish transfers to provinces, which the minister has thus far resisted in this budget. This subject requires great care because it concerns the very essence of economic balance in Canada, a fundamental condition of the concept of Confederation. We in Atlantic Canada do not consider equalization payments to be handouts but dividends legitimately earned as founding partners in the creation of this country.
As federal and provincial authorities plan together for the financial future of Canada let us be sure that their vision always remains focused on the grand original design of our country.

Mr. Speaker, Premier Rae's budget announcement yesterday will reduce conservation lands in Ontario.
The Ontario government is reducing funding for conservation authorities and removing a tax break to conservation authorities that keep these lands natural. This would encourage conservation authorities to use conservation lands for development, increase logging and even sell some of these lands in order to produce some revenue. Local conservation authorities will be unable to pay taxes on these lands and thus valuable wetlands, Niagara escarpment lands, flood plains, conservation parks and forests are threatened by these proposals.

April 29, 1993
Oral Questions
The people in Ontario should write to Premier Rae and urge him to reconsider this unwarranted decision. The environment in Ontario is not for sale.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my personal support for the ongoing conviction of the Minister of Employment and Immigration to maintain the federal government's role in manpower and training.
Effective training and human resource development are not about control but co-ordination and co-operation.
Governments must act together to remove the disincentives in the current system, eliminate the inconsistencies and pursue a national strategy which readies all Canadians to meet the challenges of tomorrow.
To pursue the efficiencies of an open and integrated market within Canada we need a training strategy which transcends provincial boundaries. That means a national approach with national standards and national input.
Provincial and local participation is important and necessary. However, let us not fool ourselves. To be successful we require a commitment and willingness to work together at all levels and not against each other.

Mr. Speaker, many times before the budget I asked the Minister of Finance whether or not he would consider closing certain tax loopholes, most notably the business and entertainment tax deduction, and some of the other tax loopholes the Auditor General identified in his report.
At one point, I even thought that the Minister of Finance was considering doing something like this, particularly given that changes have been made south of the border which have eliminated some of the excuses he had given before.
I was very disappointed to see in the budget that none of these tax loopholes were closed, not a single one. It is not just a question of not having tax increases. It is also a question of not closing any of these tax loopholes thus giving the lie once again to the real intention of the
government, which is not deficit reduction but an ideological agenda by which it keeps doing things to institutions like VIA Rail and the CBC under the cover of deficit reduction.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to draw to the attention of the House one of the themes which the federal government will consider closely during this National Consumer Week.
This year the federal government will stress the theme of consumer credit so that consumers can make decisions with full knowledge of the facts when they use the various credit instruments at their disposal.
The use of credit remains high and consumers can sometimes overextend themselves because of the falling interest rates. Some credit problems can occur if consumers do not make appropriate use of the information already available on how to use credit wisely, since they too often have easy access to credit. As a result they can draw too heavily on their credit and consumers can end up with too much debt.
Consumers are the key to a dynamic economy. This is why they must be well informed before deciding on the type of credit to use, and they must also be demanding about the quality of services provided by their lenders.
I am confident that National Consumer Week will enable Canadians to be better informed on issues which concern them, as well as on their rights and responsibilities.

years?

Is the Prime Minister prepared to admit that-based on his own comments-he and the Conservatives are guilty of keeping unemployment so high? Is he prepared to do something right now to launch a real recovery and truly lower an unemployment rate which is way too high?

April 29, 1993

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, one would hope that a government's budget would contain some vision of what the future should be. This week's budget certainly does tell something about the Conservative vision of the future, but in many ways it is a very negative and going back to the past kind of future. My question is for the Acting Minister of Finance. In just looking at transportation we see a record of privatization, deregulation, cutbacks to VIA Rail and cutbacks to airlines which have created a crisis both in number of jobs lost and in service to Canadians. Does this government have a vision of the future of transportation in this country, and what is it?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend knows that the National Transportation Agency is completing a review as has the royal commission on transportation requirements in the year 2000 in Canada. There are $3.8 billion worth of real cuts in 1993, $5.8 billion worth of real cuts in 1994, $7.9 billion worth of real cuts at the end of the fiscal framework, for a total of $30.7 billion in cuts over the five-year period, which is the largest expenditure reduction in the history of Canada.
We are not denying that; we are affirming it as a fact. We think this is a signal of confidence we are sending to the international markets of the seriousness with which we embark on a program of deficit reduction.

The basic criteria is still that all the defence policies of the Government of Canada would be reviewed with peacekeeping as the core purpose for the army, as indicated by our defence critic, the member for Labrador.
We are raising this issue today with a number of concerns in mind. One is about the Somalis who have lost their lives in recent weeks as a result of measures that are the object of an inquiry at last.

The minister has the power to order an open procedure if she wants. The minister should not be afraid of an open inquiry. We must remind the government of the promise it made for an open government in the 1984 election and repeated in 1988 by the present Prime Minister.

The persistent question is: What could we have done in order to prevent this immense human tragedy? With the benefit of hindsight perhaps some of these questions can be answered but even so in an incomplete manner.
The first answer that comes to my mind is that when Yugoslavia began to break up, and for that matter the former Soviet Union as well, an unconditional and hasty recognition of the new nations took place. This was led by Germany in particular with its immediate recognition of Croatia.
One cannot help but think that had this recognition been given more slowly with conditions attached to it such as a commitment by the western nations to adhere to the United Nations Human Rights Covenants and other major United Nations declarations of that kind, a more orderly process would have taken place in Europe. The behaviour of these new emerging nations would have been better and the transition would have been better managed. Therefore we all share a responsibility in the manner and speed in which the new nations were recognized by the west.
There is another possible answer and that is the slow and disorganized reaction particularly by the western European governments which were expected by the world community to develop a united response as the crisis began to emerge in the former Yugoslavia in particular.
Here we can definitely see that a number of decisions were made in bilateral ways or in a disjointed non-consultative manner which led eventually to the disaster we
are facing.

He has built a great reputation for this country. He has built on some of the things that have gone before and is carrying us forward into a post-cold war environment in a way that is sensitive, imaginative and very much in Canada's interest.

I was very careful not to criticize the Prime Minister, who is getting ready for a trip. She misunderstood if she thought I was questioning the right and in some cases the duty of a Canadian Prime Minister to travel abroad.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to point out first of all that I was very pleased to hear from the hon. member for Davenport who I thought for the first time produced a serious note in this debate from the other side of the House.

I am also confident that I have some answers to questions about Bosnia and other countries in that war-tom region. The hon. member raised that point in the short speech he just made.

One of the reasons I am very glad to be in this debate, despite the fact that the motion itself is ludicrous and makes no sense in any official language, is that it does allow a continuation of the national discussion on peacekeeping that I and this government launched earlier this year.
We welcome a penetrating discussion of the new and less predictable environment for peacekeeping that we face today. We want a widespread public discussion because this really is indeed one of Canada's major contributions to peace and security in the world.
Let me ask then about the role the opposition has played in this national debate. What we get from the Liberal opposition critic is a cynical and partisan motion that indicates really a very superficial interest in matters of substance. He has repeated again and again his tired old assertions that the mandates of our peacekeeping forces are confused and that our professional peacekeepers are badly equipped and badly instructed.
Nothing could be further from the truth and it is an absolutely contemptible distortion. Opposition members cannot be doing much serious thinking about this subject if that is the best they can come up with.

April 29, 1993
Supply
Further, to suggest that peacekeeping mandates are confused and unclear not only is disturbing for the families and for Canadians who care about these people, but is also totally inconsistent with the careful consideration that has been given to each and every one of our peacekeeping commitments. It is also inconsistent with the sustained diplomatic efforts we are making to ensure other governments understand those mandates as we do.
Throughout the many years during which Canada has been sending peacekeepers abroad, including under Liberal governments, successive governments have had to face the question of risk and of the role which Canada believes it should play in the world. In so doing we have developed guidelines that are weighed carefully before a decision is made to respond to a clear and precise request from the United Nations to send Canadian troops to a trouble-spot.
There has to be a threat to international peace and security. That is the first determinant. Major parties to the conflict must accept the peacekeeping mission and accept Canadian participation in it. The operation has to be linked to an agreement by the parties to work toward a political settlement. The operation must be accountable to a political authority, such as the UN Security Council. The operation must have a clear and realistic mandate and it must have a sound logistic and financial basis. Those are the tests we put forward before any of our troops are sent on any peacekeeping mission.

These guidelines have guided this government's decisions to send peacekeeping troops to Croatia, Bosnia and Somalia. As I have indicated on many recent occasions, in particular at the seminar on peacekeeping which I hosted in February 9, the circumstances under which peacekeeping is conducted have changed dramatically since the end of the cold war.
Our peacekeepers today take on new tasks, especially those of a humanitarian nature, which are particularly evident in Bosnia and Somalia. In other cases, they work alongside civilian election monitors, humanitarian agencies and policemen, as in Cambodia, to alleviate suffering and pave the way for the reconstruction of shattered societies.
The world has changed considerably in the past four years. A familiar world has suddenly disappeared, a new one is being bom among uncertainties, a resurgence of ugly nationalism and religious hatreds. We could well choose to ignore this new reality or take a comfortable back seat. This has not been the choice of this government. Our vision is to enhance Canada's reputation as a nation of experienced and trusted peacekeepers and to build upon it with thoughtfulness and imagination-as well as with a sense of compassion and care-care for the victims of conflict, and care for our soldiers.
Canadian peacekeepers are deployed when the international community has decided that they are needed and that Canada's contribution will make a difference. This must be emphasized. Support for the United Nations and the multilateral system is a pillar of Canadian foreign policy. Given our history and place in the world it has served us well.
Six years ago the United Nations was responsible for
10,000	peacekeepers and today is managing close to 50,000. That number may well double soon. It is therefore critical for Canada to ensure that the United Nations be better equipped for the task placed upon it by member states. This has been recognized by the Secretary-General who launched an urgent appeal to the international community in his agenda for peace. Canada has responded because the efficiency of the United Nations is as critical to the enhancement of peace and security in the world as it is critical to the safety of its military and civilian peacekeepers.
Moreover, Canada has provided some of its most qualified staff to the United Nations' Peacekeeping Office, including the military adviser to the Secretary-General, General Baril. Canadian officers have taken the lead in providing expert studies designed to strengthen the ability of the United Nations to do its job. One study on providing stand by forces to the United Nations has just been completed. If implemented it will enable operations to start earlier and under optimal circumstances, thus enhancing the security of troops and civilians.
Our pleas that the United Nations establish a 24 hour seven day a week situation room have been heard. The facility is being set up.
April 29, 1993

My work as minister requires full consultation with my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, and with Canada's highly professional military leaders. I assure the House that this consultation takes place on an ongoing basis.

I want to ask the Liberals if they understand how peacekeeping forces are mandated and instructed because I do not think they do. Do they seriously believe that a peacekeeping mandate is a little manual that addresses every contingency a commanding officer is likely to encounter in the field? Does my critic on the other side so misunderstand the relationship between political decision makers and military professionals that he thinks nothing can be left to the good judgment and professional competence of our peacekeepers?
It appears to me that if there is confusion and a lack of clarity, it is in the minds of those on the other side. On this side of the House, we understand the responsibilities that weigh on commanders in the field. We understand the difficult decisions they have to make in changing circumstances. Together, my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, and I go to considerable lengths to ensure that both their mandate and the resources available to them in their own estimation are appropriate to the task they have to perform.
That does not detract from the difficulty of the task, nor from the risks. However it is no service to our commanders, our peacekeepers around the world to suggest that the job of the government, let alone of the opposition critic, is to second-guess their every move.
That is why I energetically pursued discussions last week with the United Nations, the foreign ministers of the United Kingdom and Greece and the External Relations Commissioner of the European Community. It is because we recognize the partnership and the need to ensure the environment for our people on the ground. That is why I am also in frequent touch with U.S. Secretary of State Christopher. His country is looking at the role it might play for the first time in this troubled region.
I am working to ensure that our peacekeeping activities are co-ordinated with those of other governments,
Supply
for example and in particular, in the case of our allies' promise of support to Canadian troops in Srebrenica.
I also constantly remind other governments that the planning of any further military action in the former Yugoslavia must take into consideration the safety of peacekeeping forces and humanitarian workers already on the ground.
Those are the kinds of diplomatic efforts our peacekeeping forces require from government. What I find most offensive about the Liberal Party's attack is that it undermines the efforts we are making in concert with many other countries to try to move the Yugoslav conflict to the stage of negotiations.
I want to assure the people of Canada, particularly our people on the ground and the families of our peacekeepers, that we went into the former Yugoslavia with our eyes open. We joined UNPROFOR in Croatia to help monitor a ceasefire and to prevent massive bloodshed. The international community's efforts there, and I want to underline this for the House, have met with success. The so-called Sector West where Canadians are deployed is tense but it is quiet and it is the most stable in the region.
Next week I am going to visit our troops there and tell them how proud Canadians are of them. Despite difficulties in fulfilling the mandate of UNPROFOR due to distrust and hatred on both sides, there is no alternative to renewing the mandate. UNPROFOR I, with Canadian participation, has saved countless lives in Croatia and Canadians are proud to share this success.
Canada joined UNPROFOR II in Bosnia for a compelling humanitarian mission: to escort convoys of food and medicine, and to protect refugees from attack. Again this has saved thousands of lives but has tragically not resolved the conflict. No one is more aware than I of the terrible personal tragedies, the rape of women and girls, the agony at the loss of homes and loved ones.
We are in constant touch with UNPROFOR and with the United Nations in New York to ensure that our soldiers have the support and guidance they need to discharge this very difficult mandate. We have ensured the appropriate participation of Canadian military officers in the over-all command structure.
I want to reassure Canadians particularly about Srebrenica, a place where all the world is focused at the moment. On April 6 the Security Council decided to

April 29, 1993
Supply
establish a UN presence and a "safe area" there to avoid a mass slaughter of some 30,000 besieged Bosnian Muslims.
UNPROFOR decided to send a company of Canadians and brokered a demilitarization agreement between Serbs and Muslims. The mission, I want to point out very proudly, is a major barrier to further tragedy in that town.
While it is not without risks, we have examined thoroughly the safety of our troops. We are satisfied by our consultations with the United Nations and with key colleagues such as the United Kingdom and France that have offered their support and assistance if necessary.
I want to clarify the mission because, despite mistaken assertions that our 194 soldiers are there to defend thousands of unarmed Muslims against thousands of well armed Serbs, this is not the case. This is a peacekeeping situation where UN peacekeepers are asked to monitor an agreement signed by both parties. It is not their mandate to become a party to open warfare.
There is some kind of mythology that soldiers in peacekeeping missions are not well equipped. They are not well enough equipped to resist a major attack, but they are better equipped than the public has been led to believe by the sceptics opposite.
The soldiers can defend themselves and they can protect villages against rogue elements. They are trained to do so and they are equipped to do so. Should there be a massive onslaught, of which there is no indication as we speak, the peacekeepers would be backed up or they would be pulled out.
My visit to Bosnia next week may well provide me with additional insight which I will be happy to share with this House once I return. Once again I shall be in a position to personally tell our troops of our great pride in them.
I want to spend a few minutes talking about Somalia. When Canada decided to join the initial peacekeeping operation it was also in response to concerns expressed by Canadians about an appalling human disaster. Should Canada have decided to ignore the reality of starvation and banditry? This government said no. Our soldiers there, our peacekeepers there, have once again committed themselves in a way that Canadians can be proud of.
Early on it became apparent that traditional peacekeeping would not work. We agreed to join a peace enforcement operation mandated by the UN and led by the United States. We did not take this decision lightly. Once again my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, and I consulted closely to ensure that we were satisfied with all aspects of the proposed operation, its objectives and the rules of engagement. We agreed that the requirement for troops was urgent and that the concept of operations was sound.
Canada played a critical role in ensuring progress in establishing a secure environment in Somalia. Our troops fed thousands of starving women, men and children. Canada insisted-we were in the forefront internationally of insisting-that priority attention be given to disarming the gangs that preyed on the unfortunate population. Enough progress has been made that a United Nations commander can now take over from the Unified Command. When in Somalia in about 10 days, once again I shall reassure our troops there of our continued admiration and support.
My final point in this debate is that there are constructive possibilities too. The opposition has paid no attention to some of the things we are engaged in and some of the things in the Secretary-General's agenda for peace referring specifically to preventive diplomacy. In many respects that is another new frontier, a frontier in which this government has played a strong role internationally, a role that has been acknowledged by many other countries.
We have a long way to go when we talk about preventive diplomacy. We have a long way to go before we understand how to recognize signs of impending conflict, how best to cut conflicts off and how they affect national sovereignty. Some of these things can blight a generation and destroy a country as the tragic circumstances of the former Yugoslavia show if they are not headed off in advance.
Canada is represented in CSCE monitoring missions in Kosovo and in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. There, so far, we have seen greater stability because of those efforts. Likewise we have participated in preventive deployments as when we sent several
April 29, 1993

hundred troops to the same region of the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia earlier this year.
There is a lot more to be learned about how to perform this kind of role. What kind of monitoring techniques reduce tensions and restore calm? What addresses the underlying causes of conflicts? That is one direction in which I would like to see discussion in this House and in the country. So far we have not seen much constructive debate or much constructive contribution from the other side.
Early warning, preventive diplomacy and preventive deployment are tasks that do not always require the same kinds of massive forces and resources as are needed after the fact. However, they do need special sensitivity and they need to be tackled with discretion and expertise.
Those are two attributes that have marked our international reputation throughout the post-war period. However in the post cold war era, we are heading into a new environment. We are able to advance our capacities in that direction. Indeed we have a chance to add further lustre to our reputation and provide leadership for other countries that perhaps do not have the experience and the same sensitivity to ethnic differences, to self-determination and other things that Canadians really know something about.
As I said, next week I will be in Croatia and Bosnia followed by Somalia. I will meet with our people on the ground. I will have a lot of questions to ask because I believe that in sensitive operations such as these, clear and effective communication requires constant attention. We are breaking new ground. If the opposition chose, I think it could have a real contribution to make to that. So far it has not chosen to.
I will return with a livelier appreciation of the problems. I know I will not be disheartened by the attitude of our people in the field. They are facing an enormous challenge. We are fully supporting them and we are being innovative in how we do so. Peacekeeping in the nineties is a different proposition from what it was in the early days when we did lose some of our peacekeepers, but it remains an aspect of our international activities to

date through which we rediscover our national purpose and makes us even larger than the sum of our parts.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have that question from the hon. member. One thing we have not been able to do very well as a member of the United Nations or as part of the collective in the United Nations is find ways to easily end the engagements we enter into.
We can see that from Cyprus where we have been engaged for 29 years. As a result we are bringing people home because we feel that has been a major contribution to stability in the region and that others can assume those responsibilities. More important, the parties should get together. It is their own responsibility to bring that to a conclusion.
In terms of Somalia we were in for a limited period of time. As part of the enforcement mission which was obviously a bit outside the normal guidelines for peacekeeping but well within the guidelines and the charter of the United Nations, we did say we would only go in for a limited period of time.
I cannot give the hon. member a specific date but our troops will be leaving Somalia very shortly. Perhaps we

April 29, 1993
Supply
will have some leaving at the end of May. We are just looking at how that should happen or whether there will be a need for a continued deployment for a very short period afterward.
In the former Yugoslavia we have a slightly different situation. We have peacekeepers, as I pointed out, in Sector West in Croatia, we have some unarmed police who often get forgotten about who are keeping the civil peace and we also have our troops in Sarajevo and Srebrenica and other parts of Bosnia. As I suggested we have participated with a troop deployment in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and we have had observers in that region in Kosovo.
Obviously under the current circumstance it is very difficult to put a conclusion on that in terms of a date. We are urging an end to the dispute through negotiation and through trying to bring the parties together. These are all the things that are needed in order to resolve at least the dispute or the conflict or at least the tragedy even if we cannot end the hatreds and divisions that are driving the region in the foreseeable future. I understand the hon. member's concern for the timing of these missions.

I wonder if the minister would be kind enough to tell us how much she expects the operations in Somalia to cost the Canadian taxpayers.
Before she does so I would like to quote from Dr. Mahbub ul Haq. He is the head of the UN development program who said I believe in Ottawa not very many months ago: "The threat to you Canadians will come not from ideological differences but from poverty. Your 5 per cent of the world's people will have to deal with the 95 per cent in developing countries. You can stop poor people at your borders but you cannot stop poverty from spreading in the form of drugs, pollution and terrorism".
The government has cut our ODA enormously. There has been no public or even parliamentary consultation on it. It was an update, in fact a memo, entitled "An update" that decided which countries would live and which would die, so to speak.
I do not think the minister, with respect, understands that Canadians feel very strongly about these issues. Canadians feel it is moronic to spend a billion dollars in Somalia trying to relieve tragedy there when at the same time we are cutting off Uganda or a host of other countries for reasons that have never been adequately explained. I wonder if the minister might explain them today.

I would like to point out that our aid program has not been cut drastically. Indeed, it went up faster than government expenditures for quite a number of years and has really only been subject to cuts very recently.
In terms of any changes that will come to our aid program, there are a number of changing demands on it. It is not just Russia and the former Soviet Union and countries such as that. There were some decisions made by CIDA last year in its own programming made internally about how to deploy its funds within Africa.
However, I want to assure the House and the Canadian people that first of all the funding remains for famine relief and other emergencies. There is no change in our policy on that. That money is there when it is required.
Second, any changes that we have been looking at internally will be brought to the Canadian people for consultation. There is absolutely no intent to not do that.
I understand the significance of aid. The hon. member has said that it does not make any sense to cut out funding to one country and to spend a billion dollars in Somalia. Let us look at what happened in Somalia.
April 29, 1993

Without going in and creating an environment where we can feed people there is no point in having an aid budget. Obviously that is another change.
Here is one of the things that was discussed in the peacekeeping seminar that I conducted and hosted in February where we had a number of aid people. They suggested that instead of our aid program being quite independent of our peacekeeping program that we should look at providing aid following an exercise such as the one we are engaged in in Somalia. There should be greater integration between CIDA programming and our peacekeeping, peace building and democratic institution building operations. That is a point that is very well taken. It is one that I have asked our people to look into. When we are in a position to do so we will be bringing forward a discussion on what our aid budget should look like in the future. I think the hon. member will be satisfied.
Many of the non-government organizations were quite alarmed early on when they heard all these rumours and all the speculation about changes to our aid program. My point is that events in Bosnia and Somalia in particular have changed the need. Peacekeeping is not what it used to be. The question arises particularly because of attempts to deal with situations that peacekeeping did not deal with on previous occasions and which do not seem to have been envisaged by the late Prime Minister Pearson, who initiated this.
With the Moscow-Washington cold war gone the old fashioned peacekeeping operation has to be reconsidered. There was a negotiation, including the small and the great powers and the superpowers, and an agreement that a certain line would be honoured and then people were sent in as honest brokers from the most neutral countries that could be found or the most willing countries that could be found to observe, monitor and report, and by that means they would try to maintain the integrity of that demarcation or peace line.
Out of that, over a period of several decades, grew the general concept of peacekeeping which concentrated on humanitarian relief, election monitoring, civil administration, observation, fact finding, early warning, mediation and arbitration. All of those are not really military functions but they are close to military functions. They do not involve the direct use or even a serious threat of armed force.
Now we are being asked to consider preventive deployment, perhaps in Kosovo, and peace enforcement, such as a blockade on the sea and a blockade on the Danube. No plans for this have been laid down by the United Nations.
Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali is trying to lay down rules but it is not really settled yet. It is not really clear among Canadians. We are no longer locked into a fixed situation, an obligation to the United States. We are asked to do many things and we cannot do them all.
There is a strong feeling that we should select one that we could do well, which is the peacekeeping operation. That would be Canada's independent way to serve the world.
With respect to the peacekeeping operation, I want to say that we have to look to where the main conflict is and not be completely obsessed with immediate examples. The main conflict now is between the north and the south, particularly the countries of the Atlantic community that used to control most of the other countries by
military conquest and as colonies. Since World War II those other countries have achieved at least nominal political independence and are members of the United Nations. That also happens to be the division between the richest nations and the poorest nations.
In that respect I want to refer to the United Nations report on development by Dr. ul Haq. He says:
In 1960, the richest 20 per cent of the world's population had incomes 30 times greater than the poorest 20 per cent. By 1990, the richest 20 per cent were getting 60 times more. And this comparison is based on the distribution between rich and poor countries. Adding the maldistribution within countries, the richest 20 per cent of the world's people get at least 150 times more than the poorest 20 per cent.
That is obviously a recipe for trouble, and not just for the poor people. Some of them want to change their status. Dr. ul Haq pointed out when he met our committees that his opinion is that future wars will not be so much between countries as between peoples so that peacekeeping rather than policing will be what is needed.
Policing is for governing a territory. Handling disputes between peoples requires a different approach and a different technique. What we therefore need is an inquiry that is an exploration within Canada and within the United Nations on just exactly what things need to be done for peacekeeping and how to get them done.
I am not at all sure that enforcement should be part of peacekeeping. I agree with a Globe and Mail editorial that once said that this peace enforcement looks like war enforcement. This peacekeeping looks like war-making.
We do not have the clear boundary line between peacekeeping and war that we thought we had for several decades. Part of what we have to decide today is that this subject of what is peacekeeping in the new situation between the richest peoples and the poorest peoples, wherever their territorial boundaries are, is where we have to look at making our contribution toward world peace.

Mr. Ken Janies (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs) Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on the opposition motion as presented.
I want to address the claims by the opposition that members of the Canadian forces who are now on peacekeeping missions around the world have been somewhat exposed or would be exposed to some sort of vulnerability. I think that is of concern and it is important to talk about it.
The situation, of course, is dangerous. It is obvious to anyone who watches TV or reads a paper that our peacekeepers are exposed to certain dangers. To wantonly question the efforts of the men and women of the Canadian forces when they really need unity and support is on the edge of being shameless and is a concern of mine.
Before moving to the actual situation on the ground in former Yugoslavia I want to first outline for the House how the men and women of the Armed Forces are prepared for peacekeeping. I think the member for Trinity-Spadina had some concern about how we should be preparing our peacekeepers and it is important to speak to that.
There is a false impression in some quarters by other people, not the hon. member, that we can simply walk in off the street and become peacekeepers by donning berets. Of course this is not possible.
The general purpose combat skills of the Canadian forces have become more and more essential for most of the personnel we are deploying, especially those who are going to the Balkans. Not surprisingly it has been said that peacekeeping is not a job for a soldier but it is a job only a soldier can do. This is only too valid a point today.
In fact on the basis of 44 years experience on five continents the Department of National Defence rightly believes that the best peacekeeper is a well-trained soldier, sailor, or aviator who knows his or her trade.
The suggestion that the government would recklessly send a poorly trained or improperly equipped contingent

April 29, 1993
