on any mission around the world is absolute nonsense. If everyone here really thinks about it they know that.
The basic military training of our forces training for the defence of Canada or to meet the collective security obligations is the source of their flexibility, their ability to respond to critical situations and of course their discipline. These are all key attributes required for peacekeeping.
I should not go further without taking the opportunity to talk about training because the hon. member for Trinity-Spadina has concerns about that. Members of the Canadian forces believe it is the training they get that makes them the kind of peacekeepers they are.
To ensure that high quality training the Armed Forces continually evaluates the methods the hon. member was concerned about and makes needed improvements as a matter of course. Some studies have identified the need for specialized training focusing on environmental, cultural and administrative preparation. Such training is decentralized and normally tailored to the very specific missions that our peacekeepers are going on.
For example a battalion selected for duty receives mission oriented training at home and before departure. Officers to be posted as UN military observers normally receive eight days training to prepare for their duties. There is a concern about training and the hon. member is certainly right in that we do constantly train. As the hon. member mentioned there must be a kind of flexibility so we can adjust to changing times.
Even the United Nations regards basic military training as a source of many of the skills required for peacekeeping. I do not want to suggest that there is not some concern about how those in the military who are fighters become peacekeepers. They are certainly trained to be flexible and there are training schools to do all that.
The Department of National Defence also endeavours to work with, receive information from and dialogue with the United Nations with regard to training.
There is a one week indoctrination and training process conducted at CFB Montreal every quarter for all those who are designated to serve in places like the Golan Heights and Syria.
An eight day training program is held once a year at CFB Montreal for the officers warned of possible postings to existing missions as military observers. There is a three day intensive training session which is held at National Defence Headquarters in Ottawa for officers warned of immediate departure for peacekeeping operations.
Obviously, training of Canadian forces for peacekeeping is appropriate for the tasks at hand. This has been borne out by the fact that for more than four decades
90,000	Canadian men and women have been involved in keeping the peace around the world and less than 90 personnel have lost their lives. Certainly the record has been excellent. We have a tremendous reputation and considering the number of people, over 90,000 men and women, who have been involved in peacekeeping it is quite a record.
The Canadian peacekeeping experience is the collective result of our people and our Canadian forces being involved in patrols along the green line in Nicosia, clearing mines in the sands of Kuwait and patrols in the jungles of Indo-China. It is an experience which is sought after by a growing number of United Nations member states.
It is not surprising that Canada is asked to share its peacekeeping experience with other nations and has provided briefing teams. The success of our peacekeeping abilities has been noted by other countries. Canada has provided briefing teams to more than 20 different countries around the world. Members of the Canadian forces returned just late last week from such briefings in Egypt and Pakistan. We are helping other countries around the world.
Canada is a respected member of the international community and it is one of the reasons why we are always being approached by the United Nations to provide our experience and our excellence to peacekeeping missions. Other countries know this and are eager to know what makes Canada and Canadians such able peacekeepers.
Time and time again they are told that it is basic training as the hon. member from Spadina stated. It is discipline, combat skills, suitable equipment, good communications and able logistic support. All those things are part and parcel of the success of our forces.

These qualities of course are also why we are approached by both the European Community and the United Nations to provide personnel for the international efforts to bring peace to the former Yugoslavia. In fact Canada was among the first to call for international action to resolve the crisis. Canada took its place among the members of the international community and agreed to do what it could to help end this horrible conflict.
Even though experienced peacekeeping personnel were required in the former Yugoslavia, the government carefully considered the conflict in light of the criteria or guidelines which have evolved in Canada to assist the government in deciding whether or not Canada should participate in peacekeeping missions.
Besides the training and military aspects I think the opposition will be reassured to know there are also important criteria that are considered before deciding whether we will go with the mission or not.
While these criteria are clearly not absolute they have served Canada well and include a number of areas. There must be a threat to the international peace and security of the country. The mission must be linked to efforts to obtain political settlement. The mission must have a clear and enforceable mandate. There should be agreement by the principal antagonists to the presence of Canadian troops to a peacekeeping mission.
The mission must have a clearly defined concept of operations and an appropriate command and control structure. The size, equipment and international composition of the forces must be appropriate to the mandate. The mission must have an appropriate logistics concept to support the force. The mission should be accountable to a single identifiable authority competent to support the operation. The mission must have an appropriate funding arrangement. The mission must have clear rules of engagement. The risk to Canadian forces personnel must be acceptable. The mission should not jeopardize other Canadian forces missions.
There is a good long list of very important points in the criteria of making the determination to be involved.

Mr. Speaker, I too have the pleasure to take part in the debate today which has been going on since this morning on an opposition day and is focused on a motion tabled in the House of Commons by the Liberal Party which represents the Official Opposition.
We have had the opportunity to listen to hon. members from every political party about this Liberal Party's motion which, under the disguise and the pretent of holding a debate on the position of our Armed Forces in different parts of the world, and also under the disguise of discussing the purchase of defence equipment, is aimed particularly at casting or trying to cast the blame
on the Minister of National Defence who is, as everybody knows, a candidate in the leadership race for our party.
The very wording and concept of this motion is of a totally partisan nature and is aimed exclusively and specifically at attacking and discrediting the Minister of National Defence both before this House and before the Canadian public. All the speeches that were made, particularly those of the Official Opposition members, were focused on that objective. It was clear that was the ultimate and crucial objective of the Official Opposition members.
For two or three weeks the opposition has been raising in this House issues on events that occurred in Somalia involving the Canadian military. It also has been raising concerns about the safety of our Armed Forces in Yugoslavia, particularly in Bosnia, under the auspices of the United Nations.
Of course I recognize that the opposition has the right to raise these issues, but it should be done in a totally non-partisan manner and with the sole purpose of expressing concerns about the running of our military operations under the United Nations in these two countries, Somalia and Bosnia. But it always has this political drive to attack particularly the Minister of Defence.
In the last few weeks we gave full and complete answers, without hiding anything to all the questions that were asked by opposition members. All questions that were asked received very clear answers, both from the Government House Leader and the Minister of Defence, and from the Minister of External Affairs and the Prime Minister.
In order to give even more details and to clarify further the situation in Somalia, earlier this week the Minister of Defence came to this House and read a statement outlining all the relevant details that could be given at this point on the situation in Somalia. Members will recall that following the investigations conducted by the Armed Forces in Somalia into the various events referred to, the minister informed the House that she was going to establish an inquiry commission with the mandate to report its findings to her or to the person who will be Minister of National Defence when the report is tabled. This commission will have to report its

findings to the government and to the House of Commons.
Of particular concern to me is the fact that the opposition is questioning the commission's integrity and ability to look thoroughly into the incidents in Somalia. Why question the integrity of the persons who will be part of this commission when the inquiry has not even begun?
Remember that the Minister of National Defence has indicated that civilian members will be named to the commission in order to make the process more open and so that the public can have a better access to information. The Minister of National Defence-and I stress this-has had to change the rules to allow civilians in an inquiry commission on military events.
The Minister of National Defence has nothing to apologize for. She did what was expected of her. She assumed her responsibility in a professional manner, adequately and as openly as possible. She made the facts surrounding the events that occurred in Somalia known as soon as she learned about them.
We must realize that the situation in Somalia for our Armed Forces in no way resembles any situation we might find on the streets of Canadian cities. Our service people in Somalia are working in extremely difficult conditions to which they must adapt in a country that is completely foreign to them, in an extremely volatile situation where, as we know very well, various groups and factions in Somalia have been at war for years now.
Our troops, our service people serving under the United Nations, of course, have gone to that country to try to bring food supplies to people who are dying of hunger in the remotest parts of Somalia. We noticed that the action in Mogadishu did not take very long, because Mogadishu is a big, well-organized city where it was easy for our service people to get set up and organized. Then they went out to more remote regions and places where people really needed their help.
What did our service people do in Somalia? They performed their assigned tasks professionally. They did so with all their experience and with all the attention and sensitivity they need in a country where the situation is volatile. We must realize that the slightest thoughtless action by our troops or their commanders in Somalia
could have caused a great slaughter. It could have resulted in the death of thousands of Somalis and perhaps of many of our soldiers and service people as well. But with their experience and professionalism, they have done their job professionally so far, I repeat.
All day, and even all week, we have heard in the questions and comments of opposition members in the House allegations tending to discredit the work done by our service people in Somalia, and I find that hard to accept. Even if they say they are addressing the minister and the government not the troops, they are discussing painful events that occurred in Somalia under extremely difficult conditions, we must admit.
Since our troops have been in Somalia, with all they have done there, I think that the few deplorable events are not out of proportion. We must absolutely deplore it when people die, but we must realize that Somalia is a country at war. A civil war is going on in that country to which foreigners are sent to try to restore peace and at the same time send food to needy people.
I would ask the opposition members once and for all to consider the difficulties that our service people have to go through in Somalia and to think of their families here in Canada. I would ask them to have a little compassion and understanding for the work our people are doing in Somalia and for the hardship they now experience living apart from their families, because they are in hostile territory on an extremely delicate operation.
Mr. Speaker, that is why I tell you again that the motion presented by the Liberal Party today is aimed strictly at the Defence Minister. By attacking her, this motion cannot help but tarnish the reputation of our forces and we on the government side are prepared to stand up and defend our forces, our soldiers who are abroad, be it in Somalia or in the former Yugoslavia.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to say how pleased I am to be able to stand here today and talk to this particular bill. I want to thank my seconder, the member for Peterborough, for supporting me on this particular bill.
There have been a number of other individuals, such as the member from Markham, the member for Durham, and the member for Red Deer who seconded it originally who have all been very supportive of this bill.
When we look at a bill that relates to property and the right to own property I think most of us think this bill should properly be in the Constitution. I was one of those people who was disappointed that in all the discussions that took place recently throughout this country the right to property did not become part of the Canadian Constitution. I was also disappointed about other things that took place in that debate and discussion and that we were not able to make some changes.
When it was initially suggested that property rights be put into the Constitution I thought that was a good idea. I felt it was important for the Canadian public. When that suggestion came before my York-Simcoe constitutional committee which was studying the proposals it had some difficulty with it. It was made up of a cross-section of 20 to 25 people from my riding who really felt that the protection of property and property rights should properly be in the domain of elected officials.
They felt the elected officials should be responsible for making a decision. If the public were not satisfied with that decision then in the normal process of elections the public would have the opportunity to remove them or
April 29, 1993

express their displeasure at their situation or the actions they took.
I recognized that and I agreed after some discussion with my constituents, with this group of people, and I did not pursue it any further at that time.
As a result, and things have changed considerably in this country as it relates to the Constitution, I started looking into a particular situation that has arisen in my riding and looked at the history of property rights and their importance in Canadian history and the very evolution of this country.
The historical precedents in favour of property rights are really overwhelming. Philosophically, societies were initially created to collectively protect this right.
When I as an individual cannot protect myself society will do it for me and in return I will respect and protect other member's rights to property.
The right to property could be traced back to the Magna Charta of 1215. This document did not originate the right to property. It merely recognized its existence as an inherent sacred right. The Magna Charta, through its recognition of the inherent right to property, its specific rules for compensation and its commitment to protect this right at all costs, enabled all people to build a better society.
Our Constitution fails to protect property rights. The Canadian Bill of Rights, which affirms the right to property, fails to provide a method for compensation. We as a society are obliged to not only respect this right but to ensure that it is secure.
Security of this basic right is vital for a prosperous society. The right to property provides a sense of purpose and confidence. Protecting the ability to own what we make, work for or purchase is at the very heart of our market system. It drives the economy and helps it grow.
For those unable to hold intellectual properties such as patents and copyrights, owning a house, farm or piece of property allows and encourages individual Canadians to live their lives independent of the state.
Societies which deny this right do not prosper. They do not have the freedom to enjoy the fruits of their
Private Members' Business
endeavours. Inevitably, as we have witnessed in the Soviet Union and other eastern bloc countries, if the state controls what should be owned, operated and enjoyed by the people the whole economic and political system will collapse. Citizens will fight to keep the right they entrust society to protect.
Therefore not only is its protection paramount but procedures for compensation and dispute settlement must be clear to Canadians for their innate sense of security to avoid financial ruin just to protect this right.
We must continue the traditional respect for these rights which Canada affirmed internationally when it signed the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. It states that everyone has the right to own property alone as well as in association with others and that no one shall be arbitrarily deprived of this property. But it does not go far enough. Other countries strongly protect the right to property, recognizing it is essential for a free and democratic society.
We are all aware of the fifth amendment of the United States Constitution which protects property, life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Nor can property be taken away without providing just compensation. The important point here is that the fifth amendment provides compensation should it be deemed in the public good to infringe or deny the right to property.
Italy, Germany, Denmark, Finland, Sweden and many other western democracies realized the need to compensate for property loss. The Canadian Bill of Rights affirms the right of the individual to the enjoyment of property and the right not to be deprived of it except through due process of law, yet there is no mention of just compensation.
The absence of procedures for settlement of disputes when the right to property is infringed upon renders this right meaningless. A right without means for compensation allows for that right to be removed, even through the due process of law, without any system to repay affected groups or individuals for the property loss.
At present my right, which existed long before the Constitutions which should protect it, must be defended in court at my cost as an individual. The burden of cost and proof should, in my view, rest on the level of government not on the individual property owner. It is only just that the society which has been charged with

Private Members' Business
protecting this right must prove itself legitimate when it proposes to limit or deny this right.
Did you know, Mr. Speaker, that if I do not challenge the infringement of my right to property, if I do not have the financial wherewithal to take part in that legal process there is no guarantee that a government must compensate me fairly for my loss? This is a travesty and a mockery of a most sacred right.
I am certain that most Canadians would find it appalling that their right to property really holds no true strength. Without any dispute settlement or rules for compensation during an infringement of this right it is really nothing more than a motherhood statement protected at the whim of a particular government.
Those who are going to have the most difficulty defending this particular right, the individuals who do not have the capital to go to court, are the people who are going to be most affected by this type of legislation if we do not make these changes properly and do it now.
This came up most recently in my riding over a landfill issue where the provincial government quite frankly is making a land grab to build a huge mega-dump to service the needs of metropolitan Toronto. It has set the rules for compensation. It has set the guidelines. It has said to the people: "Here is how we are going to do it. Here is how we are going to make the compensation and you are going to have to live with it because we are the government and we have set up this process. We have set up this group called the IWA and it is going to set the rules for compensation".
Are those rules going to be fair? I talked to the farmers who are involved and they are not very happy with the rules that have been brought down by this particular government.
On the other hand, they are not going to be satisfied. We are suggesting that they have a right to own this property, but they are going to have to mortgage their farms and their families' future simply to hire lawyers to take on the provincial government in this particular case. That does not make a lot of sense to me if we accept that individuals have the right to own their properties.
On the other side of my riding in New Tecumseh we have a similar situation as it relates to a hydro corridor. Again the people who are going to be affected are going to have to go to court to get fair and proper compensation and they are going to have to pay the bill. They are going to have to mortgage their lands and properties. That does not make much sense to me. That is their right. They have worked for that land. I do not think we should be taking it away from them without giving them proper compensation.
It is not just the provincial Government of Ontario. A few years ago the federal government confiscated 25 per cent of the land assets north of the 60th parallel. There are probably some members in this House who remember that. It handed it all over to the state-run Petro-Canada company at that time. There was no compensation offered or given.
Guaranteeing compensation gives the citizens the bargaining power against arbitrary laws that may deny their property rights. I think there would be a totally different situation in my riding and other ridings affected right now if the government of the day knew that an individual who was going to be affected would have the right to go to the Supreme Court and get fair compensation.
It is clear that no right, including the right to property, has absolute priority over all other rights at all times. I am not suggesting that for a moment. It is important in light of this to ensure that any infringement on property rights is not arbitrary.
When the government has proved to the court that a law infringing on my right to enjoy property is legitimate, then I must be allowed to apply for compensation to the Federal Court so I can replace, at least to some degree, the loss of this right.
These amendments to the Canadian Bill of Rights will provide a mechanism for Canadians to apply for compensation to the Federal Court if their property rights have been infringed upon or denied. This is something that is not offered to Canadians now.
Section 122 relieves the individual of financial burden and the personal hardship that may occur when attempting to prove a law infringes on their right to enjoy property. The new sections that I have proposed to the Canadian Bill of Rights recognize the most basic principle of property rights. The right belongs to each individu-
April 29, 1993

al citizen of Canada. It is theirs inherently. No further claim to it needs to be made.
Canadians should therefore not be placed in a position of having to defend this right from attack. It is the government who must be responsible for proving its law does not infringe on a property right or that the legislation is a reasonable limit upon personal rights and freedoms justifiable in a free and democratic society.
By providing specific procedures for compensation and requiring governments to prove a law does not infringe or deny a right to enjoy property, a proper balance is reached between the property rights of the individual and the legitimate needs of the state.
Any arbitrary nationalization or expropriation of property by the government would be deterred. Any unilateral decision would have to be justified, not by the individual as is presently the law but by the government wishing to expropriate and infringe upon those rights.
I will just conclude by saying that Canadians' rights must be more properly protected from the imposition and unilateral authority imposed by a government maybe to meet a political agenda or a political position without due regard or fairness for the individual affected.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak generally in favour of what we are dealing with today.
Back in 1215 when you and I were just boys, Mr. Speaker, a group of English barons got together and presented King John with a list of demands. It was the Magna Charta, one of the most important constitutional documents in the British Isles.
Chapter 19 of the Magna Charta stated that no man or woman of course shall be deprived of their property except by the legal judgment of their peers or the law of the land. That was the first historic statement of property rights and the right to due process. It is part of the common law of Canada today.
The common law can, however, be superseded by a statute at any time. For example, the government of the relevant jurisdiction could pass a law requiring that all houses over 100 years old be surrendered to the state and no compensation be paid. If you owned one of those
Private Members' Business
houses you would have no recourse under the Magna Charta.
Property rights are protected in the Diefenbaker Bill of Rights. However, that Bill of Rights applies in theory only to federal statutes and has to my knowledge been applied in very few cases, most notably that of Regina v. Diybones. Areas within provincial jurisdiction such as property and civil rights are clearly not protected.
There is a rule of statutory interpretation which says that when property is taken under statute, the statute in issue is to be read as implicitly requiring that compensation be paid to the private owner. This is only a rule of statutory interpretation. Any valid statute can expressly say that no compensation is payable when property is taken. The situation was eloquently stated by Justice Riddell of the Ontario Court of Appeal in a 1909 decision: "The prohibition, thou shalt not steal, has no legal force upon the sovereign body".
Our Charter of Rights and Freedoms which is the fundamental expression of Canadian law guarantees the right of everyone to life, liberty and the security of the person. The charter does not contain the right to hold property. The contemporary version of our fundamental law lacks the provision which free men and women have considered of primary importance since time immemorial.
The admission of the right to enjoy property means that there is no guarantee of compensation if property is taken by the government, no guarantee of due process or fundamental justice and no guarantee of fair treatment by the officials with power over the economic interests of individuals or corporations.
While the right to property is expressed in various other places in our law, it is nowhere to be found in the Constitution. Section 26 of the charter recognizes that there may be rights other than those articulated in it. However, if a right is not in the charter not only does it not have the same force and legitimacy as say, the right to life, liberty and security of the person, but someone who feels wronged cannot use the enforcement section of the charter which says that laws inconsistent with it are of no force or effect.
I believe we should entrench the right to property in our Constitution. I would refer anybody who is interested to the excellent and sound brief prepared by the Canadian Real Estate Association in preparation for the

renewed Canada. It was heard in November and December 1991.
The right to hold and enjoy property provides one of the checks against undue concentration of power in government at any level. When the Americans drew up their constitution, the right of every individual to acquire and enjoy property was included. It was felt that this would give the ordinary citizen both the independence and responsibility necessary to the success of government of, by and for the people.
One way to demonstrate the significance of the right to enjoy property is to compare countries in which it does exist to those in which it does not exist and is considered to be anathema to the prevailing political philosophy.
In countries where such rights are weak or non-existent, the arbitrary power and special privileges of the elite increase and the power of the common man and woman is diminished.
Without the protection of due process, the ordinary citizen is powerless in the face of the state that exists only to perpetuate and strengthen itself and/or its elites. For example, in the former Soviet Union the individual could never say to the state or its officers: "This is mine, you cannot take it away from me". Due process and fundamental justice are but dreams to residents of the former Soviet Union.
Even in countries where the right to hold property is well accepted and understood there are of course limits on that right. Sometimes the needs of society as a whole prevail over the needs of one individual. Even if it is necessary for an individual to surrender property under the charter, that property could not be taken except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.
Section 7 of the charter, where the right to property should be included, makes that requirement. Furthermore, all statutes must be measured against section 1 of the charter which recognizes only those limits on the rights guaranteed in the charter as are demonstrably justified in a free democratic society. It is the courts that decide the balance between the private and public rights.
It is important to have a check on unlimited property rights if only because so many things can be included in the concept of "property". Property can be said to include not only land and real estate but also the fruits of one's labour, financial return, saving investments, tools of one's land, and the facilities to make these possible. There are cases in the United States where property has been held to include government benefits.
One expressed concern is that the entrenchment of property rights in the charter would undermine matrimonial property legislation providing for the division of family assets and marriage breakdown. For the most part of course it is women who struggled hard to have this type of legislation enacted, particularly that which recognizes the economic contribution of the homemaker to the family.
I believe it is in response to the inevitable challenges of division of property legislation that section 1 will come into play.
There is a firm commitment in the courts and legislatures of this country, thank goodness, to the equitable division of property in the breaking up of marriage. To use the United States as an example once more, in that country their constitution has not precluded their assemblies from enacting legislation empowering the courts to divide and compel transfer of assets on the dissolution of marriage.
That authority is considered part of the state's concern for the protection of its citizens because family assets are only divided after a full judicial hearing, that is if the parties cannot agree to what the division should be. There is a full compliance with the due process provision of the American Constitution.
I believe our courts would consider matrimonial property legislation to be a reasonable limit demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
It is vital to the health of our country in my view that the right to enjoy property be entrenched in the Constitution. What is needed is an amendment to our Constitution. As we know, the amending formula requires the House of Commons and the Senate to approve an amendment plus the legislatures of seven provinces consisting of at least 50 per cent of Canada's population. This means that at least either Quebec or Ontario must

approve such an amendment as we are talking about today as well as six other provinces.
As of several years ago, only B.C. and New Brunswick had expressed a firm commitment to the entrenchment of property rights. But I would remind members that the present Prime Minister in a letter to David Humphreys of the Canadian Real Estate Association stated: "I want to assure Canadians of my government's full support for the inclusion of property rights as an item for discussion at the next round of constitutional discussion with the provinces".
Finally, and this is where all of us come in, the legislatures must all become convinced that the Canadian people want property rights reasonably protected in the Constitution. Without a push from Canadians generally, this issue can never really go anywhere beyond the talk we are having here today.
If we believe in it we should talk to MPs, MLAs, MPPs or MNAs. We should convince them of a need for action along the lines of the motion we are discussing today. I would salute again the member for bringing this matter before Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in the debate tonight on the motion of the hon. member for York-Simcoe, Bill C-395, an act to amend the Canadian Bill of Rights (right to property).
I want to say at the outset that I do not support the bill and I will outline those reasons in a moment. I think it is important. I apologize in advance if I did not quite catch all the member's speech. I do not think that he read into the record the elements of the motion. People who are reading the transcript of this or watching either now or on the repeats would like to know exactly what it is we are debating. It reads:
Whereas a garbage dump imposed upon a community by government to resolve another city's problem will negatively affect the right of citizens to enjoy their property and farm their land;
Whereas the right of property is the foundation of society;
Whereas its protection is one of the obligations of government and its security is necessary for the existence of civil liberty and free institutions;
And whereas a law is considered a deprivation of the right of property if it deprives owners of one of the essential attributes of

property, destroys or impairs its value, restricts or interrupts its common, necessary or profitable use, hampers owners in the application of it to the purpose of trade or imposes conditions upon the right to hold or use it and thereby seriously impairs its value;
The bill goes on to detail it, but that is sort of the raison d'etre the member has offered. I can understand from previous comments he has made in the House his concern over the possibility of a garbage dump being located within his constituency as a result of a due process that has been entered into by the Government of Ontario. I can understand his concern. It is fair enough. I do not dispute that.
However, to suggest that a solution is to place in the Bill of Rights a right to property that will in effect make permanent the old belief about a man's home being his castle, that he can do whatever he bloody well pleases within his boundaries, I do not think is acceptable. I can cite a number of occasions where there are real valid reasons why individuals should not be able to do what they feel is appropriate on their property.
I will give an example. In a flood plain, a watercourse is coming through your four or five acre parcel of land and you decide to fill it in. It is your right under this bill. So what if it blocks the flow of water, so what if it disrupts the flood plain and the management of that by the conservation authority creating flooding on your neighbour's property down the road or downstream? Another example is the right to bum leaves on your property. It is your leaves, your property, your matches. That is the ultimate result of a resolution like this one.
Had the member come forward with a bill to change the Bill of Rights to say that every Canadian has a right to a job, that every Canadian has a right to be able to afford to own his or her own home and that every Canadian has a right to education, those would have been highly appropriate goals and highly appropriate things to place in a bill of rights. However, to say that a man's home is his castle and he has the right to do whatever he pleases is not acceptable.
It is also erroneous to suggest there are no protections for individuals who, I guess in the legal sense, have the right of fee simple to occupy land. There are protections. I have gone to bat for people who have had land expropriated by the province of Ontario for public purposes such as the expansion of a highway.

The process is twofold. One is whether or not they need the land and they, the public authority, have to prove they need the land. Second is the question of fair value. There are processes built in, at least in the province of Ontario-and I cannot speak for any other provinces-that when land is expropriated and if you can prove in terms of market value what other properties in the general area have gone for, you will get that fair amount. You will not necessarily get what you think it is worth, but you will get what the benchmark says it is worth, what other properties have sold for at that point in time. So there is a process out there.
We also have to recognize that governments, regardless of stripe, have not gone on a wholesale expropriation of land anywhere in the country. There are probably two exceptions: one was the decision to create the Pickering airport and the land grab there. There is no question that it was an abuse of the powers of the federal government to take action like that and not follow through, displacing the farm community and creating a real dislocation of a lot of people. That was a misuse of power, there is no question about it. I do not think this kind of amendment would in any way change that from occurring.
As for the other one, this member's government is currently doing it. It is called vesting at Canadian airports. I wonder if the member is aware that the Department of Transport, on the instructions of Treasury Board, has applied the policy of vesting so that any tenant on federal airport land, meaning somebody who has a building or has improvements, is required to give up that building at the end of their lease with no compensation whatsoever and no due process. They can extend their life there if they reinvest in it. I am overly simplifying the process but that exists today. Treasury Board has been unwilling to move beyond that policy. It has been a bit flexible, in terms of transport, of working through the rules so that it is less onerous but it still comes down to expropriation without compensation.
There is an area in which the member can do some good work to try to bring some justice to that. We do not
need a hard and fast rule in the Canadian Bill of Rights that says property cannot be touched. We have to recognize that there are times when the public good is paramount, whether it is with regard to environmental laws, labour laws or just social justice.
In the preamble of the bill it says:
-a law is considered a deprivation of the right of property if it deprives owners of one of the essential attributes of property, destroys or impairs its value, restricts or interrupts its common, necessary or profitable use, hampers owners in the application of if it to the purpose of trade-
I might want to turn my lot into an automobile junk yard. Under this bill, any rules that prevent me from doing so would be a restriction on the profitability I could make from the land, a restriction on trade. Conversely, we have seen this NIMBY approach, not in my backyard, in community after community.
After years we recognized that putting people with special needs in large institutions did not work. As we evolved from large group homes in isolated areas of our community to smaller group homes that were integrated within our community we have heard people in neighbourhood after neighbourhood say: ''Not in my backyard, not in my neighbourhood; we do not want those people with special needs; it will lower our property values; it will make our ability to turn a profit on this piece of land and house impossible". That is why I cannot support a bill like this. The ramifications go way beyond anything that I think this member was anticipating when he put forward this bill. There is no way in good conscience that I could provide the Bill of Rights with that kind of power.
